## In brief

There are two ways to learn how DNA controls gene activity. Statistical genetics compares many people and asks which genetic differences go with differences in gene expression. Sequence-to-function models, such as Borzoi, instead learn from the genome itself, predicting molecular readouts directly from DNA sequence. Along the way, these models build up internal descriptions of each stretch of sequence, called embeddings, that might describe genetic variants in terms of what they do. Whether those embeddings capture differences *between people* was not known.

We introduce EMBHER (Embedding-based Heritability), a method that measures how much of the inherited variation in gene expression these embeddings can explain. Applied to Borzoi and whole blood, the embeddings recover much of the heritability explained by people's genotypes, and far more than the model's final predictions do. Deeper layers of the model focus increasingly on functional, evolutionarily constrained sequence, and carry less information about ancestry than genotypes do.

The embeddings also explain more of the heritability due to rare variants than genotypes do. That fits with the model sharing information across variants that are each too rare to study on their own. EMBHER brings sequence-to-function models and statistical genetics together, a first step towards models that connect population variation to function.
